div.p: Checkpointing is a relatively cost effective method for achieving fault tolerance in real-time systems. Since checkpointing schemes depend on time redundancy, they could affect the correctness of the system by causing deadlines to be missed.

This paper provides exact schedulability tests for fault tolerant task sets under specified failure hypothesis and employing checkpointing to assist in fault recovery. The effects of checkpointing strategies on task response time are analysed and some insights for optimal checkpointing are provided. The emphasis here is on utilizing this analysis as an off-line design support tool.

div.head: Checkpoints
div.p: Checkpoint schemes were originally proposed for improving the reliability of database systems and similar transaction oriented systems. Here contents of the primary memory are copied onto a stable storage device from time to time. Also the system keeps a record of an audit trail, which consists of all the transactions processed after the last successful checkpoint. Upon a hardware failure, the system is restored to the last successful checkpoint and the audit trail is processed again. This scheme avoids the need to reprocess all transactions after a failure, thus improving the system availability by reducing the average processing time per transaction. Also it is highly economical as compared to hardware redundancy techniques. Several research works

[ 10][3][4][9] related to analysis of checkpointing have been reported. The focus of the above works is on probabilistic analysis of transaction oriented file or database systems for obtaining a handle on average system behaviour, whereas our work addresses hard real-time systems more specifically and focuses on deterministic worst-case analysis.

Checkpointing in a real-time system has some important differences compared to that employed in a database system. Normally a real-time task does not require an audit trail (except in the case of task which access global data), since all the data are assumed to be local upon initiation of the task. The saved state of the task, which consists of values of data variables and contents of system registers, is called a checkpoint. To ensure correctness of a checkpoint with certain failure models, an acceptance test must be executed before saving the necessary data [7]. Basically an acceptance test is checking a condition which is expected to happen if the program has successfully executed. In principle it is not intended to guarantee absolute correctness of the results and hence could be employed at diverse levels ranging from a simple reasonableness check to exhaustive verification of output parameters. Again this involves a tradeoff between how comprehensive the acceptance tests are, versus the associated design and run-time costs. Since it is highly application dependent, we will not be elaborating further on acceptance tests and will be assuming that suitable and economical acceptance tests can be devised for the class of applications we are dealing with. Tasks are allowed to exchange data via shared memory, but again an appropriate acceptance test needs to be executed before passing data to other tasks. These requirements are standard in fault tolerant systems.

div.head: Feasibility Analysis Under Checkpointing
div.p: We assume a set of n tasks, (71, 7 2 , .., T ~) in which tasks are ordered according to the assigned priorities, where 1 denotes the highest priority and n denotes the lowest priority.

Each task ~i is assumed to have a minimum inter-arrival time Ti, worst case execution time (WCET) Ci and deadline Di. Thus tasks arrival may be either periodic or sporadic. We assume that Di 5 T i f o r i = 1 , 2 , . . . , n.

Each task ri may be blocked by lower priority tasks for at most Bi units of time as a result of the operation of the Priority Ceiling Protocols. We use h p ( i ) to denote the set of tasks with higher priorities than i, (viz., 7 1 ~7 2 , .., Ti-1). Let Oi be the computation time overhead necessary to establish one checkpoint in task ~i . In fact the overhead consists of two parts, i.e, Oi = 0 : + Of, where 0 : is the overhead for performing ar? acceptance test and 0 : is the overhead for saving the system state at each checkpoint. Also there is a cost attached with restoration, which we denote by OR. This overhead needs to be added once in the response time equations. In this study, due to reasons of simplicity, we use a single factor for overheads viz., (Oi) and the restoration cost OF is assumed to be negligible.

We are primarily interested in tolerating transient and intermittent hardware and software faults can be effectively overcome by simple re-execution of the affected task or by executing an alternate action. Re-execution may have to perform some initial state restoration, the cost of which need to be included in the WCET of the task. Our analysis can account for software faults as well as transient faults in the execution engine. By execution engine we mean processor and cache. It should be noted that transient memory faults can induce permanent errors or undesirable error latencies, in which case, re-execution of the currently executing task may not be sufficient for recovery. We assume that the operating system kernel has adequate fault containment by using redundancy as well as robust data structures. We also assume a fault-free scheduler.

We assume that a fault can adversely affect only one task at a time, and it is detected at the end of that task's execution or at some intermediate checkpoint. Although somewhat pessimistic, this assumption is realistic since in many implementations task errors are detected by acceptance tests, or watchdog timers which interrupt the execution of the task once it has exceeded its budget. Meremadi and Torin

[ 5 ] have described a physical fault injection experiment, in which by using a combination of 2 software based methods and one watchdog timer, they were able to detect around 93% of the control flow errors caused by transient faults. In the case of tasks communicating via shared resources, we assume that an acceptance test is executed before passing an output value to another task by a global write operation. This is essential to avoid the domino effect [7] due to fault propagation. So in essence, we assume that Faults are detected either before a global write, or at a checkpointing time, or upon completion of the task.

div.head: Burns et a1 [2]
div.p: extended the general model for schedulability analysis by modifying the task response time recurrence equations to include Fi, which is the additional factor due to faults in response time Ri. This factor Fi depends on two parameters viz., the inter-arrival time between faults and the additional computation requirement of the fault tolerance mechanism employed. We assume a specified minimum value for inter-arrival time between faults, and checkpointing as the fault tolerance mechanism. This value for inter-arrival time between faults is either derived from past system fault data or assumed to be the worst-case value the system can cope with. If a fault occurs, the task which is being currently executed will be returned to its last checkpoint. Execution will then proceed, with the task having the same priority as before. Our analysis will be valid as long as the inter-arrival time between faults does not fall below an assumed value.

It can be seen that the schedulability of a task set under faults, can be improved if we can reduce the additional computation time requirement after the fault occurrence. In the case where we resort to re-execution of the task, the system needs the same amount of execution time upon a fault. But if we employ checkpointing we need to execute the task only after the last checkpoint which considerably reduces the additional computation requirement upon fault occurrence. Also this does not cause any deterioration in the service quality as is the case with exception handlers.

It should be noted that in a system with fixed hardware checkpointing, there is a possibility that there could be tasks which never get checkpointed. In such cases, some task's computation time could be greater than the checkpoint interval but it may never get checkpointed. This could lead to undesirable error propagations unless there is a mechanism for detection of faults at task preemption points as well. Also checkpoints happening at the middle of a shared data access cannot be ruled out. So we prefer to checkpoint a fixed proportion of the task duration rather than as a fixed proportion of the time line. Also, it should be noted that in more ad hoc systems, only a maximum checkpoint interval per task may be known.

div.head: Optimal Checkpointing Strategy
div.p: If there is no overhead for checkpointing, then we could checkpoint after every instruction. Since there is an overhead, this becomes a bounding problem. It is obvious that checkpointing will not be beneficial for tasks whose cam- putation time is lower than the checkpoint overhead.. Typically the checkpoint overhead will be much smaIler than the task computation time and hence this situation rarely occurs. However, it does provide a lower bound on the checkpoint interval. Below which, adding further checkpoints increases the response time beyond that found using our simple model for re-executing the task. div.p: One important question here is, what parameter are we attempting to optimize in our studies. In case of database applications, most of the studies were aimed at optimizing either system availability or mean response time. The objective of maximizing system availability is related to the fact that system is unavailable for users during error recovery. Mean response time is the average time a user has to wait for the completion of the transaction request. But both the above measures are of little importance when we consider a real-time application. div.head: Simulation Study
div.p: In order to obtain a good understanding of the effect of checkpointing on task response times, we conducted a sim-ulation study. Though the simulation process will be more appropriate in understanding the average behaviour, we expect that it will also provide insight for developing an optimal checkpointing strategy.
Our study consists of the following two steps:
e Generate a random task set e Conduct feasibility analysis of the task set

The task set characteristics were generated according to uniform distribution. This study was confined to task sets with only 3 tasks, since it is sufficient to provide the necessary variations due to checkpointing higher or lower priority tasks. The task periods were generated randomly in the range 501 5 T, 5 1000. For simplicity we have assumed the deadlines to be equal to periods. But the case of arbitrary deadlines can be incorporated easily into the program. The computation time for each task was selected randcmly in the range 101 5 C, 5 aT,, where a is the maximum allowable utilization per task, which we assumed to be 0.5 for this study. We have purposefully avoided smaller values to be considered for T, and C,, so that we can assume a reasonable value in the range 0-100 for the checkpoint overhead. The task priorities were assigned as equal to the task index, so that it will be an arbitrary fixed priority assignment. This can very well be modified to accommodate any other fixed priority scheme such as Rate Monotonic or Deadline Monotonic priority assignment.

Generating the following data for the study could have been done in several ways. But our selections were, Fault inter-arrival time was chosen to be the maximum permissible value, which is Mazv,(D,) (since any larger value will imply only one fault within the maximum response time of any task). If the system is not feasible with TF = Mazvj(D,), then it will not be feasible with faults occurring at any higher rate. However, the inter-arrival time of faults could very well be chosen as a random value from the permissible range Mazy, (Cj) to Mazy, (Dj).

Checkpoint overhead can be chosen as a variable depending on the task execution time or as a constant for all tasks. We have chosen it to be a constant equal to 10% of the minimum of task execution times.

Number of checkpoints can be either dependent on task execution times or could be equal to a variable. We have chosen as it as a variable which can take values from 0 to a user provided maximum value.

Feasibility tests on the above task set is performed assuming all plausible combinations of checkpoints on each of the three tasks and their response times were calculated. Using this data, 3-dimensional surface plots are also generated with the number of checkpoints on pairs of tasks on X and Y axes and response time on Z axis. A sample surface plot showing response time of task 3, with checkpoints in tasks 1 and 2 , is given in figure 1. Observations Obviously, checkpointing a lower priority task does not affect the response time of a higher priority task.
Checkpointing a higher priority task need not always bring down the response time of the lower priority task. Figure 1 illustrates this point.

At times a sudden increase in response time of a lower priority task was observed while checkpointing itself. This was observed when the overhead for a checkpoint caused another release of a high priority task.

If the maximum of checkpoint intervals is greater than the checkpoint interval of the task under consideration, then further checkpointing of that task is not effective, and can even have an adverse impact.

The problem of finding a global optimal checkpointing strategy is extremely hard, due to the complex ways in which task timing characteristics, priorities and overheads determine the response times. Also lack of an accepted single criteria for optimization is a major issue. One avenue for future work could be, the development of suitable heuristic solutions based on individual optimum values.

div.head: Summary
div.p: that checkpointing is employed for rollback and recovery. The analysis presented provides useful suggestions on probable checkpointing strategies, which can make the system schedulable in the case of unschedulable task sets. We have proved that our CP-algorithm is an optimal scheduling algorithm. We also derived analytical expressions for optimal checkpointing strategies for individual tasks. We have provided a set of observations regarding the issue of obtaining a globally optimal checkpointing algorithm.
